topic: An Introduction to Philosophy of Religion
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Vedantic Hinduism teaches the unity of atman and Brahman

options.text: Soul and god are entirely separate

'That thou art' (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7) — atman (the individual self) is identical with, or in relation to, Brahman (ultimate reality); different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship as non-dual, qualified non-dual, or dualist
Only Brahman is real; atman is illusion with no relation
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha form a connected Hindu framework

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically via realisation of the unity of atman and Brahman, or through bhakti devotion
Karma punishes only in this life
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes toward death.
